events.name: Dholki (ڈھولکی) - pre-wedding music nights
events.meaning: Informal pre-wedding singing nights held at the bride's and/or groom's family home. They start one to two weeks (sometimes several weeks) before the wedding and are often repeated over several nights. They are traditionally led by women and often women-only. Women sit in a circle on floor cushions. One plays the dholak, a small two-headed hand drum (Rekhta: ڈھولکی = small drum), and another keeps time by striking it with a steel spoon. Evenings often open with the Punjabi folk song 'Suhaag', then move on to teasing songs, couplets and dancing. There is no religious rite. Today it may use a DJ or playlist. It is purely celebratory and sets the mood for the wedding.
events.typical_colors: Bright folk colours. Truck-art palette: fuchsia #E4007C, marigold orange #FF7A00, sunflower #FFD400, parrot green #6CC24A, turquoise #00A6A6, royal blue #2453A6, all on a night aubergine. Phulkari palette: madder/rust-red base #A4282C, golden-yellow silk floss #F2B705, magenta, green. Suggested roles A (truck-art night): bg #3A0B3F, it #FFE7A3, ef #F2549B, cd #FFF3E3, ink #3A0B3F, ink2 #D6246E, acc #F5B700, fl #FF6F3C, lf #12A89D. Roles B (phulkari): bg #A4282C, it #FFE9B0, ef #F2B705, cd #FFF1D6, ink #4A1010, ink2 #C2410C, acc #F2B705, fl #E4405F, lf #2E7D32.
events.mood: Playful, noisy, homely and teasing, with a 'the party starts here' feel. Bouncy, rhythmic animation suits it, such as pulses on the drum beat.
events.motifs: Dholak with rope lacing and a steel spoon. Clapping hands with glass bangles. Colourful dupattas and parandas (tasselled braid ornaments). Phulkari darn-stitch embroidery (geometric/floral, red base, golden floss). Pakistani truck art ('phool patti': dense flowers, ornate borders, mirrors, chain and pendant fringes, birds). Mirror-work dots. Floor cushions. Paper bunting and fairy lights. Mehndi cones and mithai boxes. Animation ideas: rings pulsing out on each drum hit, a spoon tapping, bunting swinging, bangles shimmering, a truck-art border drawing itself in. If people are shown, use women's hands or faceless seated women in dupattas rather than the couple.

Urdu: 'ڈھولکی' / 'ڈھولکی کی رات' / 'صرف خواتین کے لیے' (ladies only).
Hosts: the bride's (or groom's) family, often 'the bride's sisters & cousins'. Use 'Dholki' rather than the Hindi/Bollywood 'Sangeet' as the default label.

events.name: Mayun / Mayoon (مایوں) with Ubtan
events.meaning: Pre-wedding beautification and 'seating' of the bride, held at her parents' home a few days to about a week before the wedding. Some families also hold one for the groom. Rekhta defines it as a pre-wedding rite in which the bride and groom stop going out, wear yellow and stay at home ('maaiyon bithana'). Female relatives rub ubtan (a turmeric, gram-flour, sandalwood and rose-water paste) on her face, arms, hands and feet. Traditionally this began a period of seclusion (about 8-15 days). Today it is usually one evening of ubtan, songs and dance, sometimes merged with the Mehndi, and some families skip it. The bride wears no makeup and a simple yellow shalwar kameez or ghagra with a dupatta, yellow bangles, and oiled hair braided with a paranda. Her yellow outfit is often sent by the groom's family. In Pakistan the rite is called Mayun/Ubtan, not the Indian 'Haldi'.
events.typical_colors: Turmeric/mustard yellow dominates, with marigold orange, leaf green, a little gold, and red accents (in Punjabi custom a red cloth is held over the bride). Roles: bg #E8A317 (turmeric), it #FFF8E1, ef #FFD54F, cd #FFFBEA, ink #5D3A00, ink2 #B5541B, acc #C99A2E, fl #FF8F1F (marigold), lf #4E8B2E. Evening variant: bg #3E4A12 (deep olive) with the same yellows.
events.mood: Tender, intimate and homely. A little shy and emotional (the bride's last days in her parents' home), but with giggles and songs. Warm, sunlit, softly swaying animation.
events.motifs: Bowl (katori) of ubtan. Marigold (genda) garlands and strings. A yellow or red dupatta canopy held over the bride by four women. Low wooden stool (peerhi/patri). Paranda braid. Yellow and green glass bangles. Fresh-flower or gota jewellery. Abstract turmeric smears or handprints. Green leaves, brass tray, mustard gota-lace borders. Show the bride alone (veiled or faceless) or use symbols only; the couple is not together at Mayun.
events.typical_text:
EN: 'Mayun' or 'Mayun & Ubtan' / 'With love (and a little ubtan), please join us for the Mayun of our daughter [Bride]' / '[Date] - 5:00 pm - at our residence' / 'Dress code: yellow'.
Urdu: 'رسمِ مایوں' / 'بتاریخ ... بروز ... بوقت شام ... بمقام: رہائش گاہ'.
Roman Urdu: 'Rasm-e-Mayun' / 'Peela jora, ubtan ki khushboo - aap ki shirkat ka intezaar rahega' (composed; medium).
Host: the bride's family (the groom's family for his Mayun).

events.name: Mehndi / Rasm-e-Hina (مہندی / رسمِ حنا)
events.meaning: The henna night, held one or two nights before the Baraat. It is the most colourful music-and-dance event. Henna is applied to the bride's hands and feet and stands for joy, beauty and luck. Traditionally the groom's side sent the henna and mithai to the bride's home (Rekhta: hina-bandi). Today the groom's family arrives carrying decorated thaals of mehndi and ubtan with candles. The couple sits on a stage while relatives come up one by one, give money (salami) and feed them mithai. Dance performances follow, often a friendly bride-side versus groom-side contest. Bride and groom traditionally had separate Mehndis; now a joint Mehndi in a hall is common.
events.typical_colors: The Pakistani Mehndi signature is green, yellow and orange (HSY contrasts this with Indian mehndi's reds and oranges). Hot pink/magenta and mint/peach pastels also appear. The bride wears green, yellow or orange (About Islam: green, to match the henna). Henna-stain brown is about #8B3A1A. Roles A (henna leaf & marigold): bg #0E4D2C, it #FCE8B2, ef #F4C430, cd #FFF7DF, ink #3B2A0A, ink2 #A0461F, acc #D9A62E, fl #FF8C1A, lf #7BC043. Roles B (pink & orange): bg #8E1453, it #FFE3EE, ef #FF9F1C, cd #FFF0E6, ink #4B0F2E, ink2 #E0570F, acc #F2B134, fl #FF5C8A, lf #1E9E6A.
events.mood: Exuberant, festive and teasing, with high energy and colour and movement everywhere.
events.motifs: Henna patterns (buta/paisley, vines, dots, floral rosettes) that draw themselves. Henna cones. Mehndi thaal with candles in glass holders (not clay diyas). Marigold strings and canopies. A swing (jhoola) dressed in marigolds. Patterned umbrellas (chhatris). Gota-patti flowers and mirror-work. Fresh-flower or gota jewellery (tikka, earrings, wrist gajray). Parrots, mangoes, truck-art borders, dhol, mithai trays, lanterns, rose petals. Animation ideas: a henna line drawing across a hand, candles flickering on a thaal, marigold strings dropping in, umbrellas opening.

Roman Urdu: 'Mehndi ki raat aap ke baghair adhoori hai' (composed; medium).
Host: the bride's family (the groom's family hosts the groom's Mehndi).

events.name: Nikah / Aqd-e-Nikah (نکاح / عقدِ نکاح)
events.meaning: The Islamic marriage contract and the religious core of the wedding. An imam or nikah khwan performs it with the bride's consent and two witnesses. The khutba is recited, and the bride and groom each say 'Qubool hai' (I accept), traditionally three times. The Nikahnama (contract) is signed and the haq mehr (mahr, the groom's obligatory gift to the bride) is recorded. Dua for the couple follows, and dates (chhuharay) and sweets are often distributed; jurists permit distributing dates. It may be held at a mosque (Badshahi Mosque became a popular Lahore nikah venue), at home, or at the Baraat venue, either on the Baraat day or days or months earlier. After Jumu'ah or after Asr are favoured times; a Deoband fatwa approves nikah after Asr with walima after Maghrib. The couple may sit side by side separated by a white net.
events.typical_colors: Calm white, ivory and cream with gold, plus soft pastels (mint, sage, blush, peach). Emerald or deep navy suit an evening card. Some brides wear red, white and gold. Roles A (ivory & gold on emerald): bg #0B3B2E, it #F3E9D2, ef #F6EFE2, cd #FBF8F1, ink #1F2A26, ink2 #8C6A1E, acc #C8A24A, fl #E9B8B8, lf #9CBFA6. Roles B (mint day): bg #DCEFE6, it #23413A, ef #FFFFFF, cd #FFFFFF, ink #23413A, ink2 #A27B2C, acc #C9A646, fl #F2C6C2, lf #7FB59B.
events.mood: Sacred, calm, dignified, prayerful and quietly joyful. Use slow fades and light effects rather than party energy.
events.motifs: Islamic geometry (8-point star/khatam, girih, interlocking circles). Mihrab arch and jaali lattice. Mosque domes and minarets (a Badshahi Mosque silhouette for Lahore). Crescent and stars. Calligraphy: Bismillah, Qur'an 78:8 or 30:21, 'Qubool Hai'. Nikahnama scroll with a qalam, a pair of rings, a bowl of dates and mishri. White roses and jasmine/motia (Pakistan's national flower). Hanging lanterns (fanoos) and a sheer white net canopy. Animation ideas: a geometric star drawing itself, lanterns glowing, calligraphy revealed by a right-to-left mask wipe, 'Qubool Hai' appearing three times.

(Qur'an 78:8)' / 'With the blessings of Almighty Allah' / 'Mr. & Mrs. [Bride's father] request the honour of your presence at the Nikah of their beloved daughter [Bride] with [Groom] s/o Mr. & Mrs. [Groom's father]' / 'Friday, [Date], after Asr prayer, Insha'Allah' / 'at [Masjid/Venue], Lahore' / 'Your duas are our greatest gift'.

Roman Urdu: 'Taqreeb-e-Nikah' / 'Nikah khwani: ba'd namaz-e-Asr'.
Host: usually the bride's family, or both families jointly.

events.name: Baraat / Barat (بارات) - the wedding day
events.meaning: The main and most formal event. The groom's procession arrives at the bride's venue (marquee, hall or hotel), which is hosted by the bride's family; they welcome the party with garlands and rose petals. Traditionally the groom came on a decorated horse (ghori) with dhol and dancing; today he usually comes in a flower-decked car. Before leaving home, the sehra is tied on the groom (sehra bandi), and a small nephew dressed like him (shah bala) rides along. At the venue: the nikah if it was not held earlier, then playful rituals (joota chupai: the bride's sisters hide the groom's shoes for ransom; doodh pilai: a decorated glass of milk in exchange for money), dinner, stage photos, and finally the Rukhsati. Two cards exist. The bride's family invites guests to the marriage/Rukhsati of their daughter. The groom's family invites guests to 'accompany the Baraat' of their son, giving a departure time from home.
events.typical_colors: Classic red/crimson/maroon with heavy gold zardozi. Alternatives are gold and champagne, or deep jewel tones (emerald, royal blue, plum). The groom wears ivory/off-white or gold, or maroon/black. A 2026 Lahore baraat example: ivory sherwani with a matching gold-detailed pagri. Roles A (royal maroon & gold): bg #4A0A12, it #F6E3C1, ef #7A0F1C, cd #FFF6E8, ink #4A0A12, ink2 #B3122E, acc #D4AF37, fl #C2185B, lf #1E5B3A. Roles B (crimson + emerald Mughal): bg #2B0A0E, it #F3D9A4, ef #8B1E2D, cd #FDF3E1, ink #5A0F16, ink2 #8B1E2D, acc #E2B54A, fl #D7263D, lf #0F6B4B.
events.mood: Regal, grand and ceremonial, with the splendour of a Mughal court. Drums and fireworks energy at the start, dignity on the stage.
events.motifs: Mughal palace doors, cusped arches, jharokha balconies, jaali screens. Kashi-kari tile borders (Wazir Khan Mosque palette: cobalt, turquoise, white, green, orange, yellow, purple). Pietra-dura / parchin-kari florals (tulip, poppy, iris, narcissus). Shalimar Gardens charbagh, cypresses and fountains. Sehra strands (pearls, jasmine, roses, gold tinsel). Turban with turra and kalgi. Rose and motia garlands (haar), or a currency-note garland for a rural Punjabi feel. Dhol and band, fireworks (aatish-baazi), a decorated car or white ghori, shah bala, chandeliers, a rose-petal shower, gold zardozi borders. Animation ideas: doors swinging open, a petal shower, sehra strands swaying, fireworks blooming, a gold border embroidering itself.

Roman Urdu: 'Baraat ki aamad' / 'Aap ki shirkat hamare liye baais-e-musarrat hogi'.

events.name: Rukhsati (رخصتی) - the bride's farewell
events.meaning: The bride formally leaves her parents' home or venue for her husband's home. It closes the Baraat evening, or is a separate 'Rukhsati' function when the nikah was held earlier. Rekhta defines it as farewell, specifically the bride's departure from her parents' house. It is deeply emotional, 'filled with blessings and tears'. Parents and elders make dua. In many Pakistani families a brother or uncle holds the Qur'an over the bride's head like an umbrella until she reaches the car; this is widespread, though Darul Ifta Birmingham says it has no Shariah basis. She is led to a decorated car (historically a doli/palanquin). At the groom's home his sisters and younger brother playfully demand 'entry fees'. It corresponds to the Indian 'Bidaai'; Pakistani cards say 'Rukhsati'.
events.typical_colors: The deep crimson/maroon of the bridal outfit with dusky rose and gold, set in twilight tones (plum, indigo) for a bittersweet feel. Roles: bg #24112E (plum dusk), it #F5D9E4, ef #6D2C4F, cd #FCF1F3, ink #3A1428, ink2 #9B1C3C, acc #D8B26A, fl #E07A9A, lf #3E6B57.
events.mood: Bittersweet, tender, emotional and prayerful. Slow, soft movement; a hush after the celebration.
events.motifs: A doli/palki silhouette (without bearers' faces) or a flower-decked car with rose and tuberose strings. Falling rose petals and jasmine. The bride's veil drawn forward. Parents' hands raised in dua (hands only). Lanterns and a moonlit sky, an open doorway or threshold, a trailing red dupatta. Do not animate the Qur'an as a prop.
events.typical_text: Usually one line in the Baraat programme: 'Rukhsati: 10:00 pm' / Urdu 'رخصتی: رات 10 بجے'. As its own card: 'Mr. & Mrs. [Bride's father] request the pleasure of your company at the Rukhsati of their beloved daughter [Bride] with [Groom] s/o ...'. Roman Urdu: 'Rukhsati ki taqreeb'. Closing dua: 'Allah Ta'ala is jori ko hamesha salamat rakhe' / 'اللہ تعالیٰ اس جوڑی کو ہمیشہ سلامت رکھے' (medium).

events.name: Walima / Valima (ولیمہ) - the groom's family feast
events.meaning: The marriage feast hosted by the groom's family, usually the day after the Baraat (sometimes days or weeks later). It celebrates and publicly announces the marriage and introduces the couple to society. It is a Sunnah: the Prophet (peace be upon him) told Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf to 'perform a walima, even if only with a goat' (Bukhari). Guests are urged to accept a walima invitation, and simplicity is praised. Today it is often the most polished reception (hotel, marquee or farmhouse). The bride may wear the 'moonh dikhai' jewellery the groom gifted her, and guests give salami (cash gifts).
events.typical_colors: Soft pastels and metallics: blush/peach, ivory and silver, lilac/lavender and sky blue, champagne. An evening alternative is midnight navy with champagne gold. The groom wears a grey, navy or black sherwani, suit or prince coat. A Jan 2026 example: groom in a grey sherwani, bride in a lilac lehenga with silver. Roles A (lilac & silver): bg #2A2346, it #EFE8F7, ef #CDB8E6, cd #FFFFFF, ink #2E2840, ink2 #7E5A9B, acc #BFC6CF, fl #F3C1D3, lf #A9C5B9. Roles B (navy & champagne): bg #13213D, it #F2E6D0, ef #E9DCC6, cd #FBF7F0, ink #1B2541, ink2 #8C6E4A, acc #D6BE8A, fl #E8B7B0, lf #8FAFA3.
events.mood: Graceful, refined and understated, with a calm luxury.
events.motifs: Soft florals (roses, peonies, ranunculus, jasmine), crystal chandeliers, pearl strings, fine-line arabesque or geometric frames, ribbons, a monogram of initials, candles in glass, silver foliage, a tiered floral stage arch. Use sparkles and pearls instead of champagne bubbles or glasses, which read as alcohol.
events.typical_text:
EN: Bismillah or 'Alhamdulillah' / 'Mr. & Mrs. [Groom's father] request the pleasure of your company at the Walima reception of their son [Groom] with [Bride] d/o Mr. & Mrs. [Bride's father]' / 'Sunday, [Date] - Dinner 8:30 pm - [Venue], Lahore' / RSVP. Wording attested on real cards: 'Walima Ceremony of their beloved son'.
Urdu: 'دعوتِ ولیمہ' / 'بسلسلۂ دعوتِ ولیمہ' (medium) / 'آپ کی تشریف آوری ہمارے لیے باعثِ عزت ہوگی'.
Roman Urdu: 'Dawat-e-Walima' / 'Aap ki tashreef aawari hamare liye baais-e-izzat hogi'.

events.name: Qawwali Night / Mehfil-e-Qawwali (محفلِ قوالی) - optional extra
events.meaning: An increasingly common pre-wedding evening of Sufi devotional music (qawwals with harmonium, tabla and clapping), and a Pakistani alternative to the Indian 'sangeet'. Groomsmen traditionally wear black kurta shalwar with a bottle-green patka, and the groom may wear white. Some religious families avoid music; keep Qur'anic text off music-themed cards.
events.typical_colors: Black/charcoal, emerald, gold, deep red and candle amber. Roles: bg #0F3D2E (or #0E0E0E), it #F3E3B5, ef #1E4D3A, cd #F7F1E1, ink #1B1B1B, ink2 #0F6B3F, acc #C9A44C, fl #B71C1C, lf #2E7D32.
events.motifs: Harmonium, tabla, clapping hands, shrine-style domes and arches (no saint portraits), rose petals, lanterns, dhurrie/kilim carpets, Urdu/Persian poetry calligraphy (not Qur'an).
events.typical_text: 'An evening of Qawwali in celebration of [Bride] & [Groom]' / Urdu 'محفلِ قوالی' / '[Date] - 9:00 pm - [Venue]'.

events.name: Mangni / Baat Pakki (منگنی) - engagement, optional extra
events.meaning: The formal engagement, where the families confirm the match ('baat pakki'), exchange rings and share mithai. It can be small or large.
events.typical_colors: Rose/blush, peach, ivory and gold. Roles: bg #F7E1E6, it #4A2633, ef #F2C9D3, cd #FFFFFF, ink #4A2633, ink2 #B03A5B, acc #D4A373, fl #F28CA6, lf #8DB596.
events.motifs: Pair of rings, ring box, mithai box, roses, two family houses joined by a ribbon.

card_structure: 0. Envelope or first frame (optional, personalised): guest name, e.g. 'Mr. & Mrs. ___ & family' / 'محترم ___ مع اہلِ خانہ'. A study of 100 real Pakistani cards found the guest's name was almost always written on the envelope.

1. Opening invocation, top centre. It appeared on 100% of the cards studied: Bismillah in Arabic calligraphy, the Urdu-orthography line, the English translation, or '786'. Variants to offer: Arabic, Urdu, the ﷽ glyph, the English translation, 786, 'Bismihi Ta'ala', or off. Keep it static or use a gentle fade.
2. Optional verse or hadith in small type under the Bismillah: 78:8, 30:21, 51:49, 36:36, 25:74, 'Nikah is my Sunnah', or a translation-only version.
3. Blessing line (optional): 'With the blessings of Almighty Allah' / 'بفضلِ تعالیٰ' / 'Alhamdulillah' (Walima).

4. Hosts. Found on 84% of cards, just below the opening: both parents ('Mr. & Mrs. Abdul Malik') or the father only. The host depends on the event. Bride's parents: Mehndi (bride's), Nikah (usually), Baraat/Rukhsati. Groom's parents: groom's Mehndi, 'accompany the Baraat' card, Walima. Both: 'Together with their families'.

5. Invitation formula. Found on 80% of cards, in lofty third person: 'request the honour of your presence / the pleasure of your company ... on the auspicious occasion of the [Event] of their beloved daughter/son'. Typical adjectives: beloved, auspicious, gracious, cordially.

6. Couple names. Shown on 66% of cards. Some cards hide the bride's name and give only 'D/O [father]' or 'their daughter' for modesty. Order follows the host: the host family's child comes first ('[Bride] with [Groom] s/o ...' on a bride-side card; '[Groom] with [Bride] d/o ...' on a Walima/groom-side card). Connectors: '&', 'weds', 'with'. Provide 'hide bride's name' and 'show d/o, s/o lines' toggles.

7. Programme. Present on 100% of cards and often repeated per event. Sub-parts: date + day, event name + time, venue. Write it as a chronological list, e.g. Baraat arrival 7:00 pm - Nikah 7:30 pm - Dinner 8:30 pm - Rukhsati 9:45 pm (Lahore: all must end by 10 pm). Add 'Insha'Allah' after the date. A Hijri date is optional and user-editable, because local moon sighting can shift it by a day. Weekend dates and the Nov-Feb season are typical.
8. Venue: name, area and city, with an optional map pin or QR code. Keep the venue in English even on bilingual cards.
9. Closing courtesy line: 'Aap ki shirkat hamare liye baais-e-musarrat hogi' / 'Your presence will be an honour for us' / a dua for the couple.

10. RSVP block, bottom left or right. Only 40% of cards label it 'RSVP'; the rest say 'Awaiting to welcome' or 'چشم براہ' / 'منتظرین'. Give 1-3 names with 03xx-xxxxxxx numbers. Real cards often list many relatives ('Looking forward' / family list); keep that optional and short.
11. Notes (optional): punctuality and 10 pm end time, dress code (e.g., 'yellow' for Mayun), 'Ladies only', 'Your duas are our gift', 'Separate arrangements for ladies'.
12. End card (video): 'Shaadi Mubarak' / 'Jori salamat rahe' / couple monogram / the Barakallahu lakuma dua.

VIDEO SCENE ORDER for the requested pop-up concept: (a) Bismillah alone on screen first, before any name or figure. (b) Host and blessing line. (c) Groom's name pops in. (d) Groom icon rises (turban, plus sehra if chosen). (e) Bride icon appears (dupatta with tikka, jhoomar and nath). (f) Bride's name pops in. (g) Both under an arch or jharokha with petals. (h) Event title, date, programme and venue. (i) Closing line and RSVP. (j) End card. On bride's-family cards (Mehndi, Baraat/Rukhsati), reverse c-f so the bride comes first.

Per-event emphasis. Dholki/Mayun: casual, often a home address, no verse, light invocation. Mehndi: dress-code line. Nikah: verse plus hadith, mosque, prayer-time timing. Baraat: the full programme with Rukhsati. Walima: groom's parents as hosts, 'Dinner' time, elegant tone.

Bilingual layout. English carries the logistics; Urdu gives the title, poetic lines and courtesy formulas (Urdu-English bilingual cards are common). Urdu lines need dir='rtl' lang='ur'; Arabic or Qur'anic lines need lang='ar'.

Research basis for the move model. Majeed, Sahroof & Masroor (2021, 100 cards): Opening; Parents' names; Inviting with pleasure; Bride & groom names; Programme; RSVP; Looking forward; Guest name. Yasmin et al. (2019): 7 obligatory + 1 optional moves in Urdu cards, 6 + 1 in English. Amjad & Riaz (2020): 11 moves in Baraat cards, 10 in Mehndi cards.
illustration_notes: STYLE: flat vector icons, 3-4 flat fills per figure plus one gold line accent (role acc) for embroidery and jewellery. No skin gradients. At the 340px preview, keep only 2-3 signature cues per figure (groom: turban + sehra; bride: dupatta + jhoomar + nath) so they still read. A figure should take about 25-35% of card height and never overpower the Bismillah or the names.

FACES: default to faceless (a plain skin-tone oval with no eyes, nose or mouth) or veiled (groom behind sehra strands, bride behind a sheer dupatta veil). An optional 'minimal' mode can use two closed-eye arcs and a hint of blush, with no mouth. Facelessness is a recognised modest Muslim convention (e.g. faceless dolls). Scholars differ on whether it removes the image concern: SeekersGuidance calls featureless figures a difference of opinion; IslamOnline reports Maliki/Hanbali permission when facial features are erased; Darul Uloom Trinidad still objects to featureless full figures. So also provide a 'symbols only' mode with no human figures.

SKIN & HENNA: warm South Asian browns, e.g. #E2B28C, #C98E63, #A86B45, #7E4E33. Avoid grey, very pale or 'fairness' tones. Mehndi on hands in henna brown #8B3A1A / #A0461F, drawn as vines, dots and a palm rosette.

GROOM - TURBAN (pagri/safa): stack 4-6 diagonal wrap bands crossing at the front over a visible kulla cap. The Punjabi kulla is soft and conical with a starched muslin wrap and a tall fan crest (turra/shamla) rising on one side. The Peshawari kulla is a hard dome, densely gold-embroidered, under a striped lungi. Lahore grooms typically wear a replica of the elite Punjabi pugree. Optional jewelled kalgi brooch with a small plume at the front centre. Fabric: gold tissue, ivory, maroon or rose-gold.

GROOM - SEHRA: 9-15 vertical strands hang from the turban's front band to the chest: white pearls or jasmine (motia) buds, tiny red rosebuds, and gold tinsel lines. Make it slightly wider at the bottom and give it a gentle sway. It hides the face naturally, which makes it an ideal faceless solution. It is tied at home before leaving (sehra bandi). Many modern grooms skip it, so offer a turban-only version.

GROOM - SHERWANI: knee-length coat, slightly A-line, with a high band (stand) collar and a centre placket of 5-7 round gold buttons. Add zardozi bands at the collar, cuffs and hem, optionally with scattered buti dots. Colour by event: Baraat ivory/off-white/gold, maroon or black; Nikah ivory, white or pastel; Walima grey, navy or black sherwani, suit or prince coat. Optional stole draped over one shoulder. For Baraat, a rose/jasmine haar around the neck, or a currency-note garland for a rural Punjabi feel.

GROOM - LOWER BODY & SHOES: churidar (fitted, with ruched rings at the ankle) or a straight shalwar/pajama in ivory. Khussa shoes: pointed, slightly upturned toe, gold-embroidered. Use a Peshawari chappal for Mehndi.

GROOM - OTHER EVENTS & REGIONS: Mehndi: kurta shalwar (white, mustard, bottle green or teal) with a contrasting waistcoat and a patka/stole at the neck, no turban. Qawwali: white kurta (groomsmen in black with green patkas). Nikah: sherwani or kurta-waistcoat, optional Jinnah (karakul) cap, a Pakistani national symbol. Regional variants: Sindhi ajrak shawl with Sindhi topi; Pashtun striped lungi over a gold dome kulla; Baloch white turban with no crest.

BRIDE - DUPATTA: draw it as an arch over the head covering the hair, framing the face and falling over both shoulders and arms to about knee level. Give it a scalloped gota/kiran (gold lace) border and scattered buti dots. Baraat: heavy red dupatta, optionally a second dupatta pinned over the head. Rukhsati: sheer veil drawn forward over the face, which is ideal for faceless mode. Offer a hijab-style bride variant.

BRIDE - JEWELLERY (the key Pakistani/Mughal cues): maang tikka, a chain along the centre parting with a round or teardrop pendant on the forehead. Jhoomar/passa, a fan-shaped cascade of chains and pearls pinned on one side of the head (usually the left); this is the single most 'Pakistani/Mughal' signifier. Nath, a large thin hoop on one nostril with a chain looping to the hair or ear (keep it even in faceless mode, placed at the nose position, or omit it). Bell-shaped jhumkas, a choker plus a long layered rani haar, stacks of red and gold glass bangles with kangan, optional haath phool and payal. Mehndi: swap to fresh-flower or gota jewellery (tikka, earrings, wrist gajray) in yellow, pink and white.

BRIDE - OUTFIT BY EVENT: Baraat: red, maroon or crimson. Either a flared lehenga with 2-3 wide zardozi border bands and a long kurti or choli with sleeves; or a farshi gharara (wide legs flaring from a gold gota band at the knee) with a short kurti; or a floor-length Mughal pishwas. Mehndi: yellow, green, orange or pink lehenga or gharara with mirror-work and gota. Mayun: plain yellow shalwar kameez, yellow dupatta, paranda braid, minimal jewellery, no makeup. Nikah: ivory, white or pastel with gold and a lighter dupatta. Walima: pastels (lilac, powder blue, blush, champagne) or ivory with silver, a maxi gown or lehenga, a lighter jewellery set.

POSE & COUPLE COMPOSITION: front-facing or slightly turned toward each other. Bride's hands folded at the waist or holding the dupatta edge (show mehndi), head slightly lowered. Groom upright, hands at his sides or one hand on his chest, slightly taller. Place them side by side under an arch or jharokha with a small gap; at most the bride's hand rests lightly on his arm. No embrace, kiss, dip, cheek-to-cheek, lifting, dancing-couple or lying poses.

WHO APPEARS PER EVENT: Dholki shows women's hands, bangles and dholak, or faceless seated women in dupattas, not the couple. Mayun shows the bride alone, veiled, in yellow, or symbols. Mehndi can show the bride or a joint stage. Nikah, Baraat, Rukhsati and Walima show the couple. A small shah bala (nephew dressed as the groom) is a charming Baraat extra.

SYMBOLS-ONLY KIT (for families who avoid figures): groom as a turban with turra and sehra with no face or body beneath, a sherwani on a hanger, or a pair of khussas. Bride as a dupatta-draped arch with tikka, jhoomar and nath floating (no face), a bangle stack, a mehndi hand (hands alone are widely acceptable), or gota-flower jewellery. Couple as two rings, Nikahnama and qalam, a doli/palki or flower-decked car, a mirror (aarsi), two lanterns, or interlinked monogram initials.

ANIMATION RIGGING: separate SVG groups for sehra strands (sway), dupatta edge (flutter), jhoomar (pendulum swing), bangles (shimmer), turra (slight wobble) and garland (bounce on arrival). Keep motion gentle and dignified; no comic squash-and-stretch on the bride or groom.

PALETTE MAPPING: bride outfit uses fl or the event colour (Baraat red, Mehndi yellow/green); groom sherwani uses ivory or ink2; jewellery, zardozi and khussa embroidery use acc; garlands and foliage use lf. Check that the dupatta and sherwani contrast with the card background (cd).

DO NOT draw: sindoor (red in the hair parting), mangalsutra (black-bead necklace), a red bindi without a tikka, the red-and-ivory chooda with dangling kaleere (Hindu/Sikh Punjabi), a varmala garland exchange between the couple, mandap or sacred fire, pheras, elephants, a Western white gown and veil for Baraat, an all-black bride, sleeveless, off-shoulder, cleavage, bare midriff or body-con cuts, caricatured features, skin-lightening, celebrity or designer likenesses, alcohol props, or the Qur'an held over the bride as an animated prop.
dos: Open every Muslim card with the Bismillah at top centre (100% of the 100 cards studied by Majeed et al.). Keep the existing 'Show Bismillah' toggle, defaulting to on, and offer variants: Arabic (بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ), Urdu orthography (بسم اللہ الرحمٰن الرحیم), the ﷽ glyph, the English translation, 786, 'Bismihi Ta'ala', or none.

Treat sacred text with respect. Keep the Bismillah, verses and Allah's name static or gently faded; reveal them with a right-to-left mask wipe. Keep petals, gold dust, sparkles and lanterns out of their bounding box, and keep them above people's names and imagery. Darul Uloom Deoband: paper bearing Allah's name or verses must not be desecrated. Darul Uloom Trinidad: prefer translation-only on cards that will be discarded, so offer a 'translation only' mode.

Use Qur'an text from a verified source (quran.com imlaei text, as given). Render it in Amiri, Amiri Quran or Scheherazade New. Uthmani script needs a Qur'an-capable font, and the IndoPak script familiar in Pakistan needs special fonts not on Google Fonts.

Use the right letters for each script. Urdu: heh goal ہ U+06C1, Farsi yeh ی U+06CC, keheh ک U+06A9. Arabic: ه U+0647, ي U+064A, ك U+0643. Use superscript alef U+0670 in الرحمٰن and تعالیٰ. Do not mix them within one string.

Urdu typography: lang='ur' dir='rtl', Nastaliq (Noto Nastaliq Urdu or Gulzar, both on Google Fonts), with line-height of about 2.0-2.3 so ascenders and descenders are not clipped at container-query sizes. Arabic in Naskh (Amiri, Noto Naskh Arabic). Pair Naskh with a clean serif for English. Use Kufic (Reem Kufi) only for borders and patterns, and avoid Ruq'ah on formal invites (Paperlust). Wait for document.fonts.ready before starting animations.

Animate Arabic-script names and lines as whole words or lines. For 'handwriting' or 'letter-by-letter' effects on Urdu/Arabic, use a clip-path or mask sweeping right-to-left; splitting into per-letter spans breaks the cursive joining.

Match colour schemes to events. Dholki: multicolour truck-art or phulkari. Mayun: turmeric yellow with marigold and green. Mehndi: green, yellow and orange (plus pink). Nikah: ivory or white with gold, pastels (mint, sage, blush), or emerald for night. Baraat: red/maroon with gold, or jewel tones. Rukhsati: crimson with dusk plum. Walima: pastels or ivory with silver/lilac, or navy with champagne. Real Pakistani cards most often use white, silver and cream stock with red, green and black accents.

Use authentic Pakistani, Mughal and Islamic motifs. Mughal cusped arches, jharokhas, jaali, palace doors. Islamic geometry (8-point star, girih). Wazir Khan Mosque kashi-kari tile colours (cobalt, turquoise, white, green, orange, yellow, purple). Pietra-dura florals (tulip, iris, poppy, narcissus, as in Shah Jahan-era flower studies). Shalimar Gardens charbagh, cypresses and fountains. A Badshahi Mosque silhouette for a Lahore Nikah. Truck art and phulkari for Dholki. Ajrak (crimson/indigo) for a Sindhi variant. Jasmine/motia (Pakistan's national flower), roses, marigolds, gota lace, mirror-work, lanterns.

Word the card around the host. The bride's family hosts Mehndi (hers), Nikah (usually) and Baraat/Rukhsati, and the bride is named first. The groom's family hosts his Mehndi, the 'accompany the Baraat' card and the Walima, and the groom is named first. Include s/o and d/o lines with the fathers' names, and 'Mr. & Mrs.' hosts.

Offer modesty toggles: hide the bride's name (show 'd/o [father]' or 'their beloved daughter', as some real cards do); figure mode (faceless couple / veiled / symbols only / none); a hijab-style bride variant; and 'translation only / no Qur'an text'.

Use realistic Lahore sample data. Weekend dates in the Nov-Feb wedding season. Programme times that finish by 10:00 pm (Punjab Marriage Functions Act; Lahore halls sealed for late functions in Oct 2025), with the note 'Kindly be punctual; the function will conclude at 10:00 pm'. Phone numbers in 03xx-xxxxxxx form. Fictional but typical names (bride: Ayesha, Fatima, Zainab, Maryam, Hira, Mahnoor, Amna; groom: Hamza, Ahmed, Ali, Usman, Bilal, Zain, Saad). Generic venues ('The Grand Marquee, Gulberg, Lahore').
Use Pakistani event spellings consistently: Dholki, Mayun, Mehndi (Rasm-e-Hina), Nikah, Baraat, Rukhsati, Walima. Allow user-chosen variants (Barat, Valima, Nikkah).
Provide a music-free option, or a nasheed/daf-only option, for religious families. If music is used, keep it on non-Qur'anic scenes.
Make the Hijri date optional and editable. Pakistan's dates follow local moon sighting and can differ from computed Umm al-Qura dates by a day.

Use regional variants for variety: Punjabi (conical kulla with tall turra), Peshawari/Pashtun (gold dome kulla with striped lungi), Sindhi (ajrak, topi; ajrak is presented to guests as an honour), Hyderabadi/Urdu-speaking (khara dupatta, farshi gharara), Baloch (white turban).

Use only properly licensed background imagery: own SVG art, public-domain or CC0 photos, or Wikimedia Commons files whose licence and attribution you have checked (e.g., the Badshahi Mosque category). Prefer drawn SVG versions of architecture so they scale to 4K.
donts: Don't use Hindu religious symbols or rites: Ganesha, 'Shri Ganeshaya Namah', Om, swastika, kalash (pot with mango leaves and coconut), clay diyas or puja lamps (use candles or fanoos lanterns instead), mandap, sacred fire, pheras, kanyadaan, toran with mango leaves, rangoli as a centrepiece. Lotus and peacock-feather (Krishna) motifs are borderline; avoid them as main symbols.

Don't use Hindu or Sikh bridal markers or rites: sindoor, mangalsutra, a red bindi without a tikka, the red-ivory chooda with kaleere, a varmala/jaimala garland exchange between the couple, Sikh khanda or laavaan imagery. Don't use elephants (Indian baraat and Ganesha associations; Pakistani grooms come in a decorated car or on a horse).

Don't default to Hindi or Bollywood terms: use Dholki rather than Sangeet, Mayun/Ubtan rather than Haldi, Rukhsati rather than Vidaai/Bidaai. Avoid Hindi/Sanskrit phrases such as 'Shubh Vivah', 'Shubh Lagan' or 'Swagatam'.

Don't animate Qur'anic text or Allah's name playfully (bouncing, spinning, flipping, exploding into particles, letter-by-letter scatter). Don't overlay it with falling petals or dust, place it at the bottom or below names, or put it next to jokes.

Don't pair Qur'an recitation, or on-screen Qur'anic verses, with background music. Jordan's General Iftaa' Department (2024) calls mixing the Qur'an with music a grave sin, and other fatwas call it disrespect to the Qur'an.

Don't show the Qur'an as a decorative or animated prop (e.g. held over the bride at Rukhsati). The custom is common, but Darul Ifta Birmingham says it has no Shariah basis, and a cartoon mushaf is sensitive. Don't depict the Prophet, sacred persons or saints. Avoid Kaaba imagery as wedding decoration (editorial caution).

Don't present disputed hadith as sahih. 'Nikah is my Sunnah' (Ibn Majah 1846) is hasan per Al-Albani and da'if per Zubair Ali Zai. 'Marriage is half the deen' has disputed grading. Cite the collection, not 'Sahih'. Don't treat 786 as the only invocation option, since its use is disputed.

Don't mix Arabic and Urdu letterforms (ه/ہ, ي/ی, ك/ک). Don't add letter-spacing or synthetic italics to Arabic-script text, and don't split it into per-letter spans; all of these break cursive joining and look broken.

Don't use immodest or culturally off imagery: no kissing, embracing, dipping or dancing-couple silhouettes; no sleeveless, off-shoulder, cleavage, bare-midriff or body-con outfits; no champagne, wine or toasting glasses; no nightclub vibe.

Don't put the bride in an all-white Western gown and veil, or all black, for the Baraat. Families traditionally associate white with mourning and some consider black inauspicious. Use red, maroon or gold; white and ivory suit the Nikah.

Don't show the bride's photo or name by default without an option to hide it. Don't use real celebrities' or designers' likenesses or outfits, real venue or brand logos, or copyrighted song lyrics or film dialogue.

Don't schedule sample programmes past 10:00 pm for Lahore/Punjab, or suggest multi-dish 'menus' (one-dish rule). Avoid sample dates in Muharram (first ten days especially) and Ramadan, when weddings are generally avoided (editorial caution).
Don't use the national flag as wedding decor. The star and crescent are fine as a subtle Islamic motif (common on Muslim cards), but don't make the card look political.
